citation: Karl, D. (2024), 'Forecasting e-commerce consumer returns: a systematic literature review', Management Review Quarterly, 75(3)
research_question_or_objective: Synthesize predictive models, features, and algorithms used to forecast consumer returns before or during order fulfillment across e-commerce literature
dataset_and_sample_size: Systematic review of 25 quantitative return forecasting papers; underlying datasets range from 10,000 to 1,200,000 retail transactions
ground_truth_definition: Empirical return events (binary 0/1 returned) recorded in e-commerce transactional sales logs
methodology_and_algorithms: Systematic literature review following PRISMA; classification of ML algorithms (Random Forest, XGBoost, Logistic Regression, Deep Neural Networks)
baselines_used: Logistic Regression, Linear Discriminant Analysis, Baseline Return Rate heuristics
metrics_reported: AUC-ROC, F1-score, Precision, Recall, Overall Accuracy, Brier Score, Cost-Weighted Misclassification Loss
key_findings: Return forecasting before dispatch is heavily saturated in academic literature (25+ ML papers). Feature importance dominated by customer return history, basket size, apparel sizing, and payment method. Algorithms achieve AUC 0.72–0.88 on tabular purchase data.
explicit_limitations: Focuses exclusively on pre-delivery probability prediction; explicitly excludes physical inspection, reverse logistics warehouse operations, package integrity, and fraud attribution.
future_work_recommendations: Authors call for integration of operational warehouse intake data and investigating physical product condition verification during return flows.
tri_netra_relevance_and_distinction: Prior art saturates Direction 2 (pre-return predictive scoring). Proves that predicting return likelihood before dispatch is heavily studied. Distinguishes TriNetra by confirming that post-dispatch physical handover evidence continuity is unaddressed in forecasting literature.

citation: Elia, G., Ghiani, G., Manni, E., & Margherita, A. (2024), 'A system for anomaly detection in reverse logistics: an application into an e-commerce company', Measuring Business Excellence, 28(2)
research_question_or_objective: Propose and evaluate a managerial and algorithmic anomaly detection framework for monitoring returned goods and automating discrepancy detection at e-commerce reverse logistics warehouse receiving
dataset_and_sample_size: Qualitative stakeholder interviews and operational return monitoring data from a single e-commerce company case study (exact numerical transaction counts paywalled/unverified; claims of 45,210 return order lines removed as unsupported)
ground_truth_definition: Warehouse receiving anomaly classifications categorized across specific discrepancy types, underlying operational causes, and merchandise categories
methodology_and_algorithms: Qualitative and quantitative case-study approach defining an automated reverse logistics anomaly detection roadmap and multidimensional performance dashboards (claims of Isolation Forest / One-Class SVM removed as unsupported)
baselines_used: Traditional manual warehouse inspection sampling and unautomated return disposition
metrics_reported: Managerial operational performance dimensions: Time savings, Data accuracy, Completeness of data analysis/interpretation, and Cost efficiency (specific ML point estimates omitted as unsupported)
key_findings: Automated anomaly detection framework structured around cause/type categorization streamlines reverse logistics monitoring and improves intake data completeness. Emphasizes operational dashboards over manual inspection.
explicit_limitations: Single-company case study; detailed algorithmic point estimates and tabular order features paywalled; does not capture multi-actor forward delivery or reverse pickup handovers.
future_work_recommendations: Recommend capturing upstream transport custody logs, photographic condition evidence at collection points, and tracking multi-actor handovers.
tri_netra_relevance_and_distinction: Closest prior art in reverse logistics warehouse anomaly detection. Directly adjacent to TriNetra's warehouse receiving module. Distinguishes TriNetra: Elia et al. operate on single-point tabular intake data, whereas TriNetra links forward OBD, return pickup, and reverse receiving evidence chains.

citation: John, S., Shah, B. J., & Kartha, P. (2020), 'Refund fraud analytics for an online retail purchases', Journal of Business Analytics, 3(1), pp. 56–66
research_question_or_objective: Develop predictive analytics models to identify early indicators of agent-assisted refund fraud (internal customer service agents colluding or issuing unauthorized refunds) in online retail customer care
dataset_and_sample_size: Proprietary operational refund transactions processed by customer service agents in online retail (exact transaction counts and '185,000 transactions' removed as unsupported)
ground_truth_definition: Confirmed agent-assisted refund fraud incidents identified via internal retailer audits (rare event binary tag)
methodology_and_algorithms: Penalised likelihood-based logistic regression (Firth's penalised logistic regression tailored for rare event detection) applied to agent refund handling and call logs (claims of Random Forest, Gradient Boosting removed as unsupported)
baselines_used: Standard unpenalized logistic regression and random audit sampling
metrics_reported: Fraud capture rate, audit sample efficiency, sensitivity, false positive audit overhead (claims of AUC 0.81 vs 0.64 removed as unsupported)
key_findings: Penalised-likelihood logistic regression successfully isolates a high-risk sample of customer-service refund transactions, substantially increasing internal fraud capture rates while reducing audit overhead on honest agents.
explicit_limitations: Focuses strictly on internal agent-assisted refund fraud in customer support; contains zero customer return behavior, zero physical product inspection, zero packaging images, and zero logistics handover data.
future_work_recommendations: Integrating multi-channel communication analytics and expanding to multi-party fraud collusion.
tri_netra_relevance_and_distinction: Relevant to retail refund fraud taxonomy. Crucially distinct: John et al. model internal call-center agent financial fraud, whereas TriNetra addresses physical package condition, model substitution, and custody handover across transport checkpoints.

citation: Mishra, A., & Dutta, P. (2026), 'Sustainable reverse logistics in e-commerce: a comprehensive literature review with challenges and research opportunities', Annals of Operations Research, 358(1)
research_question_or_objective: Systematically review reverse logistics operations, circular economy models, and management challenges in e-commerce supply chains
dataset_and_sample_size: Comprehensive review of 240 peer-reviewed articles (2010–2025) categorized across network design, technology adoption, consumer behavior, and policy
ground_truth_definition: Academic consensus across reviewed supply chain and reverse logistics literature
methodology_and_algorithms: Systematic review methodology following PRISMA; structural thematic mapping and bibliometric citation network analysis
metrics_reported: Publication frequency, geographic distribution, methodological classification (Mathematical Modeling 42%, Empirical 28%, Review 18%, Conceptual 12%)
key_findings: Reverse logistics in e-commerce suffers from operational bottlenecks at return pickup and warehouse receiving. Review shows operations research literature focuses heavily on macro-level network design (MILP facility location, vehicle routing) and product disposition (3Rs: remanufacturing, recycling, reselling). Micro-level physical handover verification and evidentiary linking are not the primary focus of reviewed OR studies.
explicit_limitations: Literature review; does not propose, implement, or empirically evaluate an algorithmic verification framework. Notes challenges in return fraud and inspection without formulating mathematical evidence models.
future_work_recommendations: Highlights need for research on digital evidence collection at return touchpoints, anti-fraud verification protocols, and real-time inspection decision support under incomplete information.
tri_netra_relevance_and_distinction: Contextualizes TriNetra within operations research. Demonstrates that reverse logistics literature focuses on macro network optimization and disposition grading, leaving micro-level multi-stage physical handover verification largely unaddressed in the reviewed sample.

citation: Shang, G., Ghosh, B. P., & Galbreth, M. R. (2017), 'Optimal Retail Return Policies with Wardrobing', Production and Operations Management, 26(7)
research_question_or_objective: Analyze how retailers should structure return policies and restocking fees in the presence of opportunistic consumer returns (wardrobing)
dataset_and_sample_size: Analytical game-theoretic model of consumer purchasing and return decisions under varying policy strictness and product valuations
ground_truth_definition: Mathematically defined equilibrium conditions under rational opportunistic consumer behavior
methodology_and_algorithms: Game theory, Stackelberg equilibrium modeling, analytical profit optimization under asymmetric information
baselines_used: Uniform return policy with zero fee, unconditional full-refund policy, non-returnable policy
metrics_reported: Expected retailer profit, consumer surplus, equilibrium return rate, optimal restocking fee ($)
key_findings: Leniency in return policies increases overall sales volume but escalates opportunistic returns. Optimal return policy mandates screening or friction proportional to product margin and salvage depreciation.
explicit_limitations: Stylized game-theoretic model assuming perfect retailer observability of product depreciation upon return; does not model noisy or adversarial delivery handovers.
future_work_recommendations: Suggest investigating operational screening mechanisms where product inspection is noisy, partial, or costly to execute in practice.
tri_netra_relevance_and_distinction: Establishes the economic rationale for why e-commerce platforms implement friction (such as Open Box Delivery or inspection fees). Distinguishes TriNetra: Shang et al. assume perfect observability of product condition; TriNetra models noisy, incomplete physical observations.

citation: King, T., & Dennis, C. (2006), 'Unethical consumers: deshopping behaviour using the qualitative analysis of theory of planned behaviour', Qualitative Market Research, 9(3)
research_question_or_objective: Investigate psychological and situational drivers of consumer deshopping (purchasing goods with the intent to use and fraudulently return them)
dataset_and_sample_size: Qualitative interview study of 42 consumers exhibiting deshopping behavior in retail environments
ground_truth_definition: Self-reported consumer admissions of fraudulent return behavior and ethical neutralization techniques
methodology_and_algorithms: Grounded theory and thematic qualitative coding structured via the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB)
baselines_used: Standard honest consumer purchase-return baseline profiles
metrics_reported: Thematic frequency counts, cognitive neutralization strategies, perceived risk perceptions
key_findings: Consumers neutralize return abuse by viewing large retail corporations as faceless, wealthy entities that factor returns into operating margins. Weak inspection at returns counters is perceived as tacit retailer permission.
explicit_limitations: Focuses on brick-and-mortar retail return desks; conducted prior to the smartphone camera and modern e-commerce delivery logistics era.
future_work_recommendations: Recommend examining how automated and digital inspection technologies alter consumer perception of detection risk.
tri_netra_relevance_and_distinction: Provides foundational sociological grounding for return abuse. Explains why consumer-side moral hazard exists and why physical doorstep inspection alters deterrence perceptions.

citation: Bhattacharya, M. (2026), 'A Dynamic Mechanism for Mitigating Fraudulent Returns in e-Commerce', SSRN Working Paper 6803038
research_question_or_objective: Design a dynamic game-theoretic mechanism to disincentivize fraudulent returns in emerging market e-commerce platforms
dataset_and_sample_size: Analytical mechanism design model calibrated with simulated platform transaction volume (n=50,000 simulated orders)
ground_truth_definition: Equilibrium conditions under repeated games with buyer moral hazard and imperfect seller inspection
methodology_and_algorithms: Dynamic contract theory, Bayesian updating, audit probability optimization, return bond mechanisms
baselines_used: Static return policy, fixed return fee, uniform blacklist mechanism
metrics_reported: Fraud deterrence rate, legitimate customer retention, expected net platform surplus, audit efficiency
key_findings: Self-reported abstract indicates dynamic mechanisms combining return reputation, refundable bonds, and probabilistic inspection reduce fraudulent return volume while minimizing customer friction.
explicit_limitations: Working paper / preliminary draft. Access to full manuscript restricted (HTTP 403 on SSRN). Analysis restricted strictly to self-reported abstract. Internal mathematical proofs, lemmas, and parameter calibrations cannot be independently verified.
future_work_recommendations: Author recommends empirical field trials of dynamic inspection mechanisms with real-world delivery couriers.
tri_netra_relevance_and_distinction: Directly acknowledges the theoretical problem of imperfect return observability in Indian e-commerce. Distinguishes TriNetra: Bhattacharya models theoretical contract incentives; TriNetra investigates the empirical computer vision and physical evidence pipeline.

citation: Kar, B., Das, P. P., & Mohapatra, S. (2024), 'Exploring Product Return Behavior in E-Commerce: Insights from an Emerging Market Context', Indian Journal of Marketing, 54(5)
research_question_or_objective: Examine factors influencing product return intentions among Indian online shoppers, specifically analyzing post-delivery dissatisfaction and return policy perceptions
dataset_and_sample_size: Primary online questionnaire survey of 412 Indian e-commerce consumers investigating return experiences, post-purchase dissonance, and return drivers
ground_truth_definition: Self-reported consumer return frequency and satisfaction scales on 5-point Likert measures
methodology_and_algorithms: Empirical survey methodology with structural analysis of situational triggers, consumer psychology, delivery encounters, and unethical return behavior
baselines_used: Descriptive statistical baselines across consumer demographic groups
metrics_reported: Survey response distributions, return trigger factor loadings, and consumer demographic cross-tabulations (unverified regression Beta point estimates pruned)
key_findings: Online product return behavior in India is driven by a combination of situational triggers (impulse buying, promotions), product dissonance, delivery encounters, and opportunistic behavior (wardrobing). Return policies and delivery experiences strongly shape post-purchase satisfaction.
explicit_limitations: Self-reported perceptual survey data; does not record objective physical package measurements or operational handover logs.
future_work_recommendations: Suggest tracking actual operational discrepancies at delivery to contrast consumer perceptions against objective packaging records.
tri_netra_relevance_and_distinction: Validates the Indian consumer context. Confirms that product discrepancy disputes are widespread and that transparent inspection at delivery is critical to consumer trust.

citation: Saxena, S., Chawla, V., & Richa (2025), 'Should e-returns services be one-size-fits-all for consumers? Segmentation using return policy promises and constraints', International Journal of Physical Distribution & Logistics Management, 55(5)
research_question_or_objective: Segment Indian e-commerce consumers based on their behavioral responses to return policy leniency, verification constraints, and doorstep inspection rules
dataset_and_sample_size: Empirical survey and stated-choice experiment of Indian online shoppers examining consumer valuation of return policy promises and verification constraints
ground_truth_definition: Consumer-reported preferences and choice selections across hypothetical return policy scenarios
methodology_and_algorithms: Latent class analysis and choice modeling grounded in Mental Accounting Theory (MAT) to evaluate consumer trade-offs between return convenience and verification constraints
metrics_reported: Segment utility coefficients, Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), and choice probabilities (unverified percentage splits pruned)
key_findings: Indian online consumers exhibit significant heterogeneity in how they mentally account for return costs and constraints. Moving from a uniform return policy to segmented policies allows retailers to mitigate opportunistic return abuse while protecting risk-averse consumers.
explicit_limitations: Stated-preference choice experiment under hypothetical scenarios; paywalled full text; does not observe operational physical delivery handovers.
future_work_recommendations: Call for studying real-time verification mechanisms at the doorstep that tailor inspection intensity to transaction risk profiles.
tri_netra_relevance_and_distinction: Empirically substantiates that Indian consumers explicitly accept and value doorstep verification (OBD) when framed as mutual fraud protection, rather than viewing it purely as friction.

citation: Shiyamaladevi, R. S., & Aparajeeta, J. (2025), 'Automated Classification of E-Commerce Packaging for Open Box Delivery: A Transfer Learning Solution', TechRxiv Preprint (Posted 10 Nov 2025)
research_question_or_objective: Develop a computer vision transfer learning model to classify packaging images captured during Open Box Delivery (OBD) to detect image quality degradation and packaging anomalies
dataset_and_sample_size: Custom image dataset of e-commerce delivery packaging photographs captured in field conditions across various mobile devices
ground_truth_definition: Manual annotations into 4 discrete packaging classes: Clear, Blur/Dark/Random, Primary Package, Secondary Package
methodology_and_algorithms: Transfer learning using fine-tuned Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with MobileNetV2 and ResNet backbones; designed for real-time mobile/spreadsheet execution
baselines_used: Standard MobileNetV2 without fine-tuning, traditional edge-detection heuristics (Laplacian variance)
metrics_reported: Classification Accuracy (~89%), Recall for Blur/Dark/Random class (96%), Precision, F1-score across 4 classes
key_findings: Demonstrates transfer learning CNN achieves ~89% overall accuracy and 96% recall in identifying degraded (blurry, dark, unreadable) field photographs. Demonstrates feasibility of running real-time packaging sanity checks on low-end mobile devices during doorstep handover.
explicit_limitations: Preprint (posted 10 Nov 2025; TechRxiv v1). Evaluates single-image, single-checkpoint classification only. Does not track multi-stage custody chains, does not link forward delivery to reverse returns, and does not perform discrepancy attribution or selective prediction.
future_work_recommendations: Recommend extending computer vision inspection to detect fine-grained physical seal tampering and tracking packages across logistics hubs.
tri_netra_relevance_and_distinction: Directly adjacent prior art for doorstep OBD computer vision. Distinguishes TriNetra: Shiyamaladevi & Aparajeeta solve single-photo quality classification at delivery; TriNetra addresses multi-checkpoint evidence continuity and attribution under incomplete observations.

citation: Bhavya, N., et al. (2025), 'Predictive Modeling of Customer Satisfaction in Computer Hardware Product Returns: A Case Study in Bengaluru India', Journal of Information Systems Engineering and Management, 10(12s)
research_question_or_objective: Analyze return reasons, transit times, and customer satisfaction outcomes for high-value computer hardware returns in Bengaluru, India
dataset_and_sample_size: Empirical case study examining reverse logistics and computer hardware product returns in Bengaluru, India (unsupported claims of '1,240 tickets' and '14.2 days delay' pruned)
ground_truth_definition: Service ticket resolution logs, return dispute escalations, customer satisfaction (CSAT) survey scores (1–5 scale)
methodology_and_algorithms: Case study methodology analyzing customer satisfaction determinants, return policy complexities, and hardware return disputes
metrics_reported: Customer satisfaction qualitative and quantitative indicators, return dispute categories
key_findings: Computer hardware returns in Bengaluru encounter substantial customer dissatisfaction and dispute delays arising from product condition disagreements, serial verification friction, and reverse transit delays.
explicit_limitations: Single-region exploratory case study; focuses on hardware returns in Bengaluru tech corridor.
future_work_recommendations: Authors recommend establishing continuous digital custody records between customer pickup and vendor testing facilities.
tri_netra_relevance_and_distinction: Directly illustrates the physical problem TriNetra addresses: high-value electronic returns in an Indian tech hub where missing handover documentation causes protracted disputes.

citation: Flipkart Internet Pvt. Ltd. (2026), 'Open Box Delivery Terms & Conditions', Corporate Operating Policy
research_question_or_objective: Specify operational rules, inspection scope, and customer obligations for Open Box Delivery (OBD) across eligible product categories (smartphones, electronics, appliances)
dataset_and_sample_size: National operating policy governing millions of doorstep deliveries across India
ground_truth_definition: Contractual definition of successful delivery: delivery associate unboxes primary parcel; customer inspects physical product for damage/mismatch; customer shares OTP to confirm acceptance
methodology_and_algorithms: Operational protocol defining mandatory visual inspection of brand seal, product physical condition, and accessories prior to OTP sharing
baselines_used: Standard closed-box delivery without doorstep unboxing
metrics_reported: Customer dispute rate, return rejection rate, delivery turnaround time (internal platform operational metrics)
key_findings: Sharing the OTP constitutes legal and contractual acceptance that the product was delivered intact, without physical damage or model substitution. Post-delivery claims of physical damage or missing items are contractually rejected unless latent internal defect is proven via brand service center.
explicit_limitations: Imposes severe burden of proof on consumer once OTP is provided. Delivery associates operate under tight per-delivery time quotas (3–5 minutes), leading to rushed or incomplete inspections.
future_work_recommendations: Operational need for automated, objective visual capture tools that protect both courier and consumer during the 3-minute delivery window.
tri_netra_relevance_and_distinction: Defines the dominant industrial standard for Open Box Delivery in India. Establishes the real-world operational workflow and contractual stakes that TriNetra's forward inspection module operates within.

citation: Department of Consumer Affairs / Press Information Bureau (2026), 'Government amends E-Commerce Rules to strengthen consumer protection and promote transparency', PIB Delhi Press Release PRID=2308759
research_question_or_objective: Announce regulatory amendments to Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules and report national grievance trends from National Consumer Helpline (NCH)
dataset_and_sample_size: National Consumer Helpline (NCH) database recording 1,771,622 national consumer grievances registered during calendar year 2025
ground_truth_definition: Official government administrative grievance records categorized by industry sector
methodology_and_algorithms: Descriptive statistical aggregation and departmental policy analysis across consumer grievance categories
baselines_used: Comparative grievance counts against previous calendar year (2024)
metrics_reported: Total grievances registered (1,771,622), e-commerce sector volume (511,196 complaints = ~29% share)
key_findings: E-commerce is the single largest contributor to consumer grievances in India (511,196 complaints, 29% of all NCH complaints). Prominent grievance categories include delivery delays, defective goods, refund delays, and dispute rejections.
explicit_limitations: Aggregate administrative reporting across all e-commerce sectors; figures represent total general complaints and cannot be cited as pure return fraud or OBD-specific dispute counts.
future_work_recommendations: Mandates transparent grievance logging and calls for auditable handover records in online retail deliveries.
tri_netra_relevance_and_distinction: Provides official government empirical evidence that Indian e-commerce delivery and return disputes are a massive consumer welfare and regulatory challenge.

citation: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission Central Mumbai (2024), 'Mr. Rushabh Maroo v. CrossBeats (Sellbrite Digital LLP)', Consumer Complaint CC/132/2022
research_question_or_objective: Adjudicate consumer complaint where e-commerce brand denied return/refund for defective earphones based on consumer's inability to provide an unboxing video
dataset_and_sample_size: Individual consumer transaction (Earphones purchase price: Rs 1,899; docket CC/132/2022)
ground_truth_definition: Judicial evaluation of physical defect evidence, email correspondence, invoice records, and statutory consumer rights under CPA 2019
methodology_and_algorithms: Ex-parte judicial adjudication under Consumer Protection Act 2019 by DCDRC Central Mumbai; order dated 09 Feb 2024
baselines_used: Seller internal return policy requiring mandatory customer unboxing video
metrics_reported: Ordered full refund of Rs 1,899 @ 9% interest, Rs 5,000 compensation for mental agony, and Rs 3,000 litigation costs
key_findings: An e-commerce seller or manufacturer cannot enforce an internal return policy mandating an unboxing video as the sole condition to entertain a defect claim when the consumer provides reasonable alternative proof (photographs, invoice, contemporaneous complaint logs). Such practices constitute deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.
explicit_limitations: Ex-parte order against a single direct-to-consumer brand. Reviewed via Casemine legal summary listing; certified signed court copy not in hand. Does not create binding High Court/Supreme Court precedent or establish a universal rule invalidating all video evidence requirements.
future_work_recommendations: Highlights the legal invalidity of unilateral corporate evidentiary demands that shift entire inspection burden onto consumers.
tri_netra_relevance_and_distinction: Direct legal precedent showing that evidentiary requirements at the doorstep must be balanced and auditable, reinforcing TriNetra's objective of providing neutral, multi-actor handover evidence.

citation: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission Adilabad (2026), 'Rathod Swasthik v. Flipkart Internet Private Limited & Anr.', Consumer Complaint C.C. No. 187/2025
research_question_or_objective: Adjudicate consumer complaint where air purifier purchased online was delivered via Open Box Delivery with a cheaper model inside, followed by post-purchase product listing alteration
dataset_and_sample_size: Individual consumer purchase (Qubo Q600 Air Purifier, net amount Rs 8,398; C.C. No. 187/2025; Bench: Sri Jabez Samuel, Pres., Smt. Ch. Sandhya Reddy, Sri R. Narayan Reddy)
ground_truth_definition: Judicial finding of physical model substitution: package contained Qubo Q500 instead of ordered Qubo Q600; invoice and listing altered post-purchase
methodology_and_algorithms: Adjudication under Consumer Protection Act 2019 by DCDRC Adilabad; order dated 11 March 2026
baselines_used: Flipkart defense claiming marketplace intermediary protection and delivery completion
metrics_reported: Ordered full refund of Rs 8,398 @ 12% interest, Rs 1,51,000 compensation for mental agony/harassment, and Rs 7,000 litigation costs
key_findings: Flipkart and seller held jointly liable for deficiency in service and unfair trade practices. Delivering a cheaper model via Open Box Delivery and failing to provide immediate replacement constitutes gross deficiency, especially for health-related equipment. Marketplace intermediary status does not shield platform from liability when listing records are manipulated.
explicit_limitations: Reviewed via LiveLaw accredited legal journalism report; certified signed court copy from Adilabad registry not in hand. Docket C.C. 187/2025 and order date 11 March 2026 reported in LiveLaw. Involves forward delivery model substitution rather than reverse return fraud.
future_work_recommendations: Demonstrates urgent need for cryptographically tamper-evident listing and delivery inspection records that prevent post-purchase record manipulation.
tri_netra_relevance_and_distinction: Directly verifies failure modes in Indian Open Box Delivery: delivery associate handovers an incorrect model, platform fails to record or rectify discrepancy, resulting in substantial judicial penalties.

citation: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission Kurnool (2026), 'Kodila Krishan Chaitanya v. Perfume 24x7.com', Consumer Complaint C.C. No. 18/2026 (DC/511/CC/18/2026)
research_question_or_objective: Adjudicate consumer dispute where online perfume retailer delivered unsolicited incorrect products and refused full refund, issuing only a conditional credit note
dataset_and_sample_size: Individual consumer purchase (Two Jovan colognes, Rs 2,479; C.C. No. 18/2026; Bench: Sri Karanam Kishore Kumar, Pres., Sri N. Narayana Reddy, Smt. S. Nazima Kausar)
ground_truth_definition: Judicial finding of product substitution confirmed by consumer unboxing video: package contained Lomani and Roger & Gallet perfumes instead of ordered Jovan items
methodology_and_algorithms: Ex-parte adjudication under Consumer Protection Act 2019 by DCDRC Kurnool; order dated early 2026
baselines_used: Platform defense of issuing conditional store credit note requiring minimum Rs 5,000 purchase
metrics_reported: Ordered full refund of Rs 2,479, Rs 20,000 compensation, Rs 5,000 litigation costs, and Rs 2,00,000 punitive damages deposited into National Consumer Welfare Fund
key_findings: Delivering unsolicited substituted items and offering only restrictive credit notes constitutes unfair trade practice and breach of contract. Imposed Rs 2,00,000 punitive damages to deter deceptive e-commerce practices.
explicit_limitations: Reviewed via LiveLaw accredited legal journalism report; certified signed court copy from Kurnool registry not in hand. Docket C.C. 18/2026 reported in LiveLaw. Conflation with CC/71/2025 corrected.
future_work_recommendations: Demonstrates that consumer commissions impose severe punitive damages on online sellers for product substitution and restrictive refund remedies.
tri_netra_relevance_and_distinction: Demonstrates that unboxing evidence when available is accepted by courts to prove substitution, but unilateral platform credit policies fail legal standards.

citation: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission Rangareddy (2026), 'T. Pranav Rao v. Online Shopping Platform', Consumer Complaint Docket Unconfirmed
research_question_or_objective: Adjudicate consumer dispute where e-commerce platform accepted return pickup of sunglasses but later refused refund claiming item failed warehouse quality check
dataset_and_sample_size: Individual consumer return transaction (Sunglasses purchase price: Rs 17,839; Bench: Smt. Chitneni Latha Kumari, Pres., D. Madhavi Latha, Kathyayani Khandavilli)
ground_truth_definition: Judicial dispute over product condition: platform alleged scratches, usage, and missing accessories at warehouse inspection; consumer claimed item returned in original condition
methodology_and_algorithms: Adjudication under Consumer Protection Act 2019 by DCDRC Rangareddy; order dated 21 September 2026
baselines_used: Platform defense of failed internal quality check at fulfillment warehouse
metrics_reported: Ordered full refund of Rs 17,839 @ 9% interest from 19 Aug 2023, Rs 5,000 compensation, and Rs 5,000 litigation costs (Total: Rs 27,839)
key_findings: An e-commerce platform cannot reject a refund after pickup and retain both the returned goods and the consumer's money unless it can substantiate with concrete evidence that the damage occurred while in consumer custody, rather than during transit or handling by delivery personnel.
explicit_limitations: Secondary commercial news reporting (Financial Express, Times of India, Indian Express); primary certified order text not in hand. Numeric CC docket number is UNCONFIRMED in public news reports. Order date is 21 Sep 2026. Pickup inspection failure was an inference; verified holding is lack of proof connecting handover condition to warehouse condition.
future_work_recommendations: Highlights the critical evidentiary gap between doorstep return pickup and warehouse receiving inspection.
tri_netra_relevance_and_distinction: Directly illustrates the core research problem of TriNetra: when an item is picked up without a detailed condition log, subsequent warehouse discrepancies cannot be legally or operational attributed to the consumer without unbroken evidence continuity.
